note: A ratio, not a count. Absolute survivor counts rise with every
line added -- new code means new mutants, so a healthy change
with good tests would trip an absolute ratchet. The score below
is killed / (killed + survived): it stays comparable as the
codebase grows and only moves when tests get better or worse.
Not every survivor is a gap. About a quarter only change a log
or error message, which nothing asserts on by design. Others are
equivalent: `if not mismatched` decides when the read-back loop
exits, not what it returns, so killing it would mean asserting on
timing -- a worse test than the mutant is a risk.
Mutants with no covering test are excluded from the score rather
than counted as failures: the tests that drive a module through a
real subprocess load the original source, so a mutation run says
nothing about what they cover. See
docs/decisions/0005-mutation-testing-scope.md.
0.65 -> 0.67 (2026-08-19), and this is the largest rise so far,
against the largest growth so far: 2726 -> 3745 mutants, over a
0.688 -> 0.685 with 0.4.0's EQ family, and most of the fall is a
property of the measurement rather than of the tests.
`_eq_registers` alone carries 117 survivors -- the largest count of
any function in the codebase, ahead of `build_arg_parser`. Three of
them were applied by hand and run against the full suite:
prefix = None            import error, every test fails
"XX/eqXX" in the path    one test fails
tag "I" instead of "i"   one test fails
All three are killed by tests that exist. mutmut selects the tests
that *cover* a mutant from runtime coverage, and `_eq_registers`
runs at module import inside the `UCX2 = Device(...)` literal, which
is attributable to no test in particular. So the register table --
the largest body of pure data in the project -- scores as though
nothing tests it.
This is the opposite of the 0.728 problem recorded above. There the
score flattered the suite because uncovered mutants were excluded;
here it understates it because covered mutants are not attributed.
Both are reasons to read survivors rather than the number.
What reading them actually found: no new gap in the behaviour-
carrying code. The survivors in `_register_for` and
`nested_families` are `split("/", 1)` against `rsplit` or
`split("/", 2)`, which are equivalent while no path remainder has
two slashes; the rest are message text. One real looseness turned
up and was fixed: `settable_nested` answered for childless options,
so `[gain:input:3]` was rejected only by a second guard elsewhere.

0.69 -> 0.71 (2026-08-22), and this rise is a *denominator* change,
not better tests. ADR 0015 exempts the register table from mutation:
it is built at import time, which mutmut cannot attribute to a

159 survivors left the denominator; killed moved by 9. registers.py

min_score follows floor_note's own rule rather than the rise: set at
the measured score rounded down, so the policy neither fails nor
nags. The reason it is safe to move now and was not before is that
the erosion mechanism is gone -- auto level, low cut and crossfeed
are the same shape as dynamics and will add their rows inside the
exemption, so they cannot walk the score down 0.005 at a time.

0.6.1 (2026-09-05): 0.713 -> 0.714, and the interesting number is
not_covered, which fell 82 -> 50. The 0.6.1 fix made
`_apply_and_verify` apply a config that declares no route, and the
unit test written for that rule is the first test to drive the
function *in process*. Everything reaching it before went through
the subprocess integration tests, which load the checked-out source
and not the mutant (ADR 0005), so its mutants scored as covered by
nothing at all.
32 mutants therefore entered the judged pool for the first time, and
the first run judged 19 of them survivors: the test asserted that
apply_routing had been called and that a thread came back, so the
ports handed to the apply, the stop check given to the verifier and
the thread's target, name and daemon flag could all be mutated in
silence. Reading them is what the nightly run is for, and it worked
exactly as ADR 0005 says it should -- the score would have been fine
either way.
The strengthened test kills all 19, confirmed twice: by re-running
those mutants by name, and by this clean full run, in which no
`_apply_and_verify` mutant survives. The aggregate moved 15 rather
than 19 between the two runs, so four kills were lost elsewhere in
the same interval; run 1's per-mutant results were not kept, so they
cannot be attributed. Timing-dependent mutants drift by a few either
way here, which is the standing reason this file says to read the
survivors rather than the number.
0.6.1 baseline named the last 50 mutants with no covering test --
_await_backend_port, _install_stop_handlers, one dead function --
and this release drove the two helpers in process and deleted the

Reading the survivors of the new code found one defect and three
gaps, all fixed before the release commit: usb_revision accepted hex
digits and then called int() on them (a bcdDevice of 0a01 would
have raised; BCD is decimal, and the code says so now); the port
wait's stub ignored its arguments; the reload's stop-wait had no
timing assertion; the device-table warnings were not held to naming
what is modelled. The remaining survivors in that code are message
text and a `>=`/`>` on a monotonic deadline.
How this number was produced, because it is not one clean run: the
full run (75 min, cache cleared, 03:02-04:18) judged 5172 mutants at
3687 killed / 1477 survived / 0 not covered, score 0.714. The fix in

switch lock, the atomic marker and the phase wait. Two findings
about the measurement itself, and both are worth more than the
number.
First, mutmut 3.7 leaves decorated functions unmutated. The switch
lock was a @contextlib.contextmanager generator, so the loop the
no-interleave guarantee rests on was outside the full run entirely:
zero mutants, which reads as nothing to test. It is a plain
generator wrapped at assignment now, and has 41.
Second, the by-name re-run after that change judged 21 of the 41
survivors, among them a mutant that switches the lock off -- which
the lock tests kill when run by hand. mutmut's incremental stats
re-trace the tests it already associates with a changed function,
plus new tests. A function that is new under its name has no
associations, and its callers had not changed, so one new test was
traced for it. With mutmut-stats.json cleared the same mutants were
attributed 21 tests and 8 survived. Reading those found one real
gap: the 'waiting for it' line could repeat on every 0.1 s poll,
300 lines over the wait, and nothing asserted it said so once. It
does now, with the lock file's mode beside it.

floor_note: The gate is min_score - tolerance = 0.72. That is the number that
matters: the score may not fall below it. min_score is set at the
measured score rounded down to the hundredth, so the policy neither
fails nor nags on the run it was recorded from -- a baseline that
prints 'raise me' on every CI run teaches people to ignore it.
